book: 304 - Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House

chapters.file: ch07 - How to Use this Book in a Philosophy Course.md
ch09 - The Talking Cure for Our Culture.md
chapters.relation: William Young argues that South Park stands in the Socratic-Platonic tradition and that its critics repeat the charges (impiety, corrupting youth) that condemned Socrates in the Apology. Kyle and Stan's dialogues over euthanizing Stan's grandpa model Socratic questioning and thinking from others' perspectives, while Cartman's thoughtless, imitative cruelty illustrates Arendt's banality of evil (Eichmann). Young adds a Freudian reading in which the show's vulgarity works like joke-telling to release repressed drives, so the crude cartoon actually serves the examined life.

Robert Arp uses South Park's cartoon Johnnie Cochran and his 'Chewbacca Defense' from 'Chef Aid' to teach basic logic: premises, conclusions, deductive versus inductive arguments, and validity/soundness versus strength/cogency. The Chewbacca Defense exemplifies the red-herring fallacy, and other episodes illustrate hasty generalization, slippery slope, false dilemma, appeal to inappropriate authority, and ad hominem. The chapter's subject is informal logic and fallacy theory rather than a single named philosopher or taxonomy concept.

David Kyle Johnson uses Stephen Colbert's 'wikiality' and 'truthiness' to attack individual and cultural relativism, arguing (via the correspondence theory of truth and counterexamples like slavery and Nazi Germany) that truth is not relative to persons or cultures. He deploys Locke's critique of 'enthusiasm' to show gut thinking is circular, and invokes Socratic admission of ignorance against the claim of a 'right to your opinion.' The upshot is a method: defend beliefs with argument, be agnostic when evidence is lacking.

chapters.file: ch13 - Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress.md
chapters.relation: Henry Jacoby channels W.K. Clifford's 'ethics of belief' through South Park's Stan Marsh, who debunks John Edward, holistic healers, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the believer and that faith is belief without evidence. The chapter distinguishes prudential from evidential reasons and dismantles Pascal's Wager using episodes like 'Cartmanland' (why would a good God torment nonbelievers?) and 'Do the Handicapped Go to Hell?' (which religion?). Stan's speech to Edward's audience frames uncritical belief as mental laziness that slows the progress of mankind.

Matt Lawrence uses The Matrix to stage the skeptical problem, running Descartes's dream argument and evil-demon method of doubt (the Matrix as a technological demon) and even a 'Matrix within the Matrix' to show Morpheus cannot know he is awake. Descartes's cogito supplies the one certainty that survives radical deception. Lawrence then draws on Russell's analysis of the red chair to argue against naive realism: color, texture, solidity, and shape are appearances, so even setting aside the Matrix we cannot know the world in itself.

chapters.file: ch15 - “You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”.md
chapters.relation: Eric Silverman uses Battlestar Galactica's Adama, who lies that he knows Earth's location, to run the Gettier problem: Starbuck's true belief that Earth exists rests on a false justification (that Adama knows), so it is justified-true-belief without being knowledge. He tests testimony via Goldman's reliabilism (sight is unreliable for telling Cylons from humans) and the Hume/Locke/Plantinga debate over testimony's epistemic role. He closes with James's 'will to believe': faith in Earth is a forced, momentous choice where agnosticism forfeits meaning, so belief without certainty can be reasonable.

chapters.file: ch17 - The Role of Matter Biology or Function.md
chapters.relation: Matt Lawrence uses The Matrix to survey theories of mind, arguing the 'brain-stimulation' premise favors materialism over Descartes's dualism (which alone easily explains Neo's mind-body separation at the Train Station but lacks empirical support and an interaction mechanism). He explains reductive versus eliminative materialism (Churchland's denial of folk-psychological 'beliefs' via Tastee Wheat) and then Searle's biological emergentism (the beer-can thirst machine) against functionalism (Lewis's Martian pain; Agent Smith's seamless transfer into Bane). He concludes the films are best read functionally, making sentient machines genuine minds.

Jason Southworth uses Wolverine's repeated memory erasures to test Locke's memory (and connected-memory) criterion of personal identity, arguing that on Locke's view a new 'person' inhabits Wolverine's body each time his memories are wiped, until House of M restores them all. He then deploys Jamie Madrox, whose duplicates share and re-merge memories yet act as distinct agents, as a real-comics version of Parfit's fission case, pushing Parfit's conclusion that identity requires physical (brain) continuity. Because Wolverine's healing factor constantly rebuilds his brain, the moral is to 'be slow to judge' whether a character is the same person who acted before.

chapters.file: ch19 - Time Travel and Fixed Time.md
chapters.relation: Jeremy Pierce analyzes prophecy and destiny in Harry Potter, distinguishing fallible from infallible prophecies and cataloguing how a Seer might access a fixed or open future (raising Aristotle's sea-battle problem about future truths). He argues Trelawney's two 'real predictions' are not merely likely guesses and considers self-fulfilling readings (via Alexander of Aphrodisias and Oedipus), which he rejects since the prophecy did not force Voldemort's choice. Reading Rowling's denial of 'destiny' against her fixed-time treatment of time travel and the improbable luck that fulfills the prophecy, he suggests the story fits a fixed future guided by providence better than libertarian openness or sheer coincidence.

chapters.file: ch20 - “Cyborgs Don’t Feel Pain. I Do.”.md
chapters.relation: Greg Littmann asks whether the Terminators are 'people,' testing three criteria: passing as human, thinking, and feeling. The T-101, T-1000, and T-X repeatedly pass Turing Tests, giving behavioral evidence of thought, but Littmann recasts Searle's Chinese Room as the 'Austrian Terminator' to argue behavior never proves genuine understanding. He then argues personhood requires conscious experience (what it is like to be a Terminator), and takes the films' red- and blue-tinted first-person 'Terminator's-eye view' shots as evidence the machines really are conscious, so humanity's extinction need not end personhood.

chapters.file: ch22 - Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy.md
chapters.relation: David Kyle Johnson frames Kyle's loss of faith in 'Cartmanland' (Cartman's undeserved happiness plus Kyle's hemorrhoid) as the logical and evidential problem of evil, then tests South Park's answers against real theodicies. He rejects the Book of Job answer and Chef/Edwards/Calvin's 'God benefits from our suffering,' examines greater-good and Augustine's free-will defense (only free acts are good), and notes the free-will defense fails for natural evil. He presents John Hick's soul-making theodicy, echoed by the show's Jesus ('life is about overcoming problems'), as covering both moral and natural evil, while conceding the sheer amount of evil still fuels the evidential problem.

Daniel Gallagher uses Lost's Rose, who insists 'I just know' her husband lives and the island cured her, to apply Aquinas's account of faith as 'mid-way between knowledge and opinion.' Drawing on Plato's episteme/doxa distinction and Aquinas's God/'first truth' conceptual distinction plus the five ways, he argues reason can demonstrate that God exists while faith (a grace) grasps what reason cannot. Rose exemplifies both the sin of presumption (mistaking faith for knowledge, treating the island as God's certain instrument) and, by contrast to Charlie's acedia, robust faith, so the chapter urges keeping faith and reason harmonized rather than conflated.

chapters.file: ch24 - “You Have to Believe in Something”.md
chapters.relation: Jason Eberl and Jennifer Vines use Battlestar Galactica's Baltar (skeptic) and Caprica Six/Roslin (believers) to debate God's existence, presenting Aquinas's five ways (unmoved mover, uncaused cause, governance) against a self-explaining big bang, and noting Baltar's self-serving faith resembles Pascal's Wager. They raise the problem of evil, answering with Augustine's free-will account of moral evil and Hick's soul-making theodicy (via Hume's faulty-architect analogy) for natural evil. Writing as a theist and an atheist, they argue meaning survives without God in human solidarity ('the gods shall lift those who lift each other'), and that faith and reason can share common ground.

chapters.file: ch26 - But Isn’t It Only Natural.md
chapters.relation: Don Adams uses Heroes' superpowered characters (who could commit perfect crimes like Gyges with his invisibility ring) to argue Plato's case that virtue is its own reward. He maps Plato's tripartite soul onto the characters: Claire's thumos (spirit/honor) tempered by logistikos (reason) yields courage and wisdom, while Sylar's ruling appetite (his hunger for powers) is intemperance and injustice that makes his life spin out of control. Reading justice as psychic health, and glossing the 'Pagan Golden Rule' (help friends, harm enemies, but enemies may become friends), Adams argues it is 'only natural' for even the powerful to be virtuous rather than exploit others.

Sean McAleer uses the British Office to teach Aristotle's virtue ethics, treating wit as a virtue that is a mean between the vices of buffoonery (excess) and boorishness (deficiency). David Brent is the buffoon, 'the slave of his sense of humor,' who jests inappropriately; Gareth is the boorish literalist who cannot take or get a joke; Tim is the ready-wit whose ironic humor is appropriate to the situation, exercising practical wisdom (phronesis). McAleer argues virtue is about acting and feeling appropriately (not mere moderation), that Aristotle's morality is broad enough to include humor as part of flourishing (eudaimonia), and that, like humor, virtue is noncodifiable.

Mark White asks why Batman doesn't kill the Joker, using the question to contrast utilitarianism (kill one to save the Joker's future victims) with deontology (killing is wrong regardless of consequences), and Batman's own agent-centered refusal. He runs Foot and Thomson's trolley problem and the transplant surgeon case, then modifies them: the Joker is the guilty one who created the danger, his future victims are uncertain, and killing him would be 'prepunishment' for crimes not yet committed. White, a self-described deontologist, concludes the case is genuinely hard and admits great good might have come from killing the Joker, using comics as thought experiments about killing to prevent future killing.

J. Robert Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as an apparent consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) who sacrifices millions of New Yorkers for the greater good, and Rorschach as an apparent deontologist ('I shall not compromise'), then argues neither is true to his stated theory. Utilitarianism is critiqued through Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ever ends' (the infinite future defeats the calculus) and its trouble grounding rights, while Rorschach's hypocritical, dichotomous, disrespect-for-persons stance is shown to be fascism, not Kant's categorical imperative (universalization and treating persons as ends). Loftis contends the deeper target is authoritarianism itself: the corrupt superheroes show that ethical theories are rationalizations of power, so no one should be entrusted with too much of it.

holes.name: Informal Logic and Fallacies
holes.what: The study of argument structure (premises/conclusions, deductive vs. inductive, validity/soundness and strength/cogency) and of informal fallacies such as red herring, hasty generalization, slippery slope, false dilemma, appeal to inappropriate authority, and ad hominem.
holes.why: Chapter 2 is entirely a logic-and-fallacy lesson built on the Chewbacca Defense; the taxonomy has no concept covering argumentation or fallacies, so its central topic maps to nothing.
